content: Respondent-driven sampling (RDS) is a method used to gather data from populations that are difficult to access, such as those at high risk for HIV. This method is particularly useful for collecting information on HIV serostatus, CD4+ T-cell counts, viral load, and other sexually transmitted infections (STIs). However, bio-behavioral surveys (BBS) are only one of several data sources that inform the understanding of HIV epidemics in key populations. Other sources include population size estimation, mapping, HIV case surveillance, cohort studies, program-based data, and upstream data on policy, stigma, and discrimination. These guidelines are not designed for general population or household-based surveys, as other resources are available for those purposes. Instead, they serve as a comprehensive resource for conducting BBS, focusing on practical aspects of survey implementation. The guidelines are structured into three main sections, each divided into chapters, covering survey preparation, implementation, and data analysis. The first section, Survey Preparation, is the most extensive and addresses stakeholder involvement, formative assessment, ethical considerations, survey instrument development, biomarker considerations, eligibility criteria, and population size estimation methods. It also discusses sampling strategies, sample size calculation, data management, and data collection procedures. Practical aspects such as developing standard operating procedures (SOPs), ensuring adequate human resources, and conducting staff training are also included. The second section, Survey Implementation and Quality Assurance, emphasizes monitoring and field supervision during survey execution, data management, and specific considerations for cluster surveys and RDS. Supplementary materials, such as appendices, questionnaire modules, indicators, and a glossary, are provided to support survey activities. The third section, Data Analysis and Use, focuses on analyzing survey data, disseminating findings, evaluating survey implementation, and sharing data for public use. The guidelines aim to ensure that data collection is standardized, accurate, and relevant to the needs of populations at risk for HIV. The data instruments have been updated to include questions on the continuum of care and are organized into modules focused on specific topics. This modular approach allows users to tailor data collection to local priorities and the needs of target populations. Core variables are also available in ready-to-use electronic formats. Standardized indicators facilitate comparisons of the HIV epidemic across different time points, locations, or populations. These indicators align with those used by the UN and other global organizations involved in HIV funding and programming. The supplementary materials include resources such as references for further reading, examples of protocol checklists, survey consent language, and data analysis commands for commonly used software packages. These updated guidelines aim to improve the collection of detailed, accurate, and relevant data among at-risk populations, ultimately enhancing HIV services, advocacy, and policymaking. Stakeholders play a critical role in survey planning and implementation. They include individuals or organizations with an interest in the survey, such as government agencies, development agencies, academic institutions, service providers, NGOs, community-based organizations, donors, community leaders, and members of the target population. Stakeholders contribute to the success of BBS by ensuring the survey design aligns with local realities, encouraging participation, and providing resources or services to facilitate implementation. Early engagement with stakeholders often leads to greater use of survey results for informing services, policy, and advocacy. Support from the target population is essential, and investigators should involve influential members early in the process to seek input on survey content and communicate how the data will be used. Service providers, including clinicians and NGOs, can offer valuable insights into the local context and encourage participation due to their close relationships with the target population. National officials should take a leading role in selecting target populations, variables of interest, and types of analyses, as well as disseminating the data. Leadership by a national body increases the likelihood of producing high-quality surveys that meet the country's needs and result in widely used data. Stakeholders can also help ensure the safety and security of surveyors and participants, particularly in sensitive contexts such as prisons or areas with high levels of stigma. In summary, these guidelines provide a detailed framework for conducting bio-behavioral surveys, emphasizing the importance of stakeholder involvement, ethical considerations, and practical implementation strategies. By following these guidelines, investigators can collect high-quality data to inform effective HIV prevention and care strategies.
